Stories include a charade, little footmarks in the snow, a day at the castle, faithful little Ruth, and a mother's Christmas excuse. Greenwood contrasts German grand dukes' daughters, East Indian princesses on elephants, and Turkish princesses in satin trousers with English princesses in castles. Against them she sets true-born American girls, who heard the bells of peace and mourned President Lincoln. A swapped-babies confession drives one tale of changed cradles.
27075-here-and-now-story-book-two-to-sev:
Lucy Sprague Mitchell's Here and Now Story Book, published in 1921 with illustrations by Hendrik Willem Van Loon, gathers experimental stories for two- to seven-year-olds. The tales were written for children of the City and Country School and the nursery school of the Bureau of Educational Experiments.

A foreword by Caroline Pratt and an introduction explain the educational basis: content fitted to personal activities, told in motor and sense terms. Stories like Marni Takes a Ride repeat simple patterns, with pails of nuts and marbles going bingety-bang, crickety-crack, in words children can act out.
2730-long-odds:
H. Rider Haggard tells this story as he heard it from his old friend Allan Quatermain, called Hunter Quatermain in South Africa. One evening at the place Quatermain had bought, the hunter told a tale of a wager against odds that seemed impossible.

Long Odds turns on a gamble, a hunt, and a debt of honor, with the African bush as its stage. Haggard writes in Quatermain's voice, dry and modest, letting the adventure speak. The story delights as a short, sharp sample of his art, where courage is measured against a long price.
2732-ballads:
William Makepeace Thackeray gathers his ballads in this volume, from the Chronicle of the Drum to Abd el Kader at Toulon, the Caged Hawk. The King of Brentford's Testament, The White Squall, and Peg of Limavaddy follow, with a May Day Ode and the Ballad of Bouillabaisse.

The Mahogany Tree, The Yankee Volunteers, and Mrs. Katherine's Lantern show Thackeray's range, from satire to sentiment. His verse is easy, witty, and musical, written for singing and reciting. The book offers a lighter Thackeray, rhyming his age with a smile. Thackeray sings history, satire, and sentiment in turn.
27514-a-handful-of-stars-texts-that-have:
F. W. Boreham published this book of texts that have moved great minds with the Abingdon Press in New York and Cincinnati in 1922. It follows A Bunch of Everlastings as a companion, and its introduction quotes Caliban crying for a handful of stars.

Boreham gathers a few of those stars, one text per chapter, from William Penn, Robinson Crusoe, and James Chalmers to Sydney Carton, Hudson Taylor, and Michael Faraday. Catherine Booth, Uncle Tom, and Francis d'Assisi appear too, with a final chapter called Everybody's Text. Each essay shows how one passage shaped a life. The book suits devotional and literary readers alike.
27874-foot-prints-of-travel-or-journeyin:
Maturin M. Ballou published Foot-Prints of Travel, or Journeyings in Many Lands, in Boston with Ginn and Company in 1889. Aimed at young readers, the book covers a broad field briefly, drawing on his earlier travel volumes and on notes from countries those books did not mention.

Ballou urges readers to use good maps while reading, so that geography is impressed pleasantly on the mind. The chapters conduct readers across continents with Captain Cook on the frontispiece, offering entertainment and information in the Victorian tradition of travel for youth. Ballou's earlier volumes included Due-West, Due-South, Due-North, and Under the Southern Cross.
2819-barrack-room-ballads:
Rudyard Kipling's Barrack-Room Ballads gather his poems in the voice of the ordinary British soldier, known as Tommy, in India and on campaign. The first series of 1892 and the second of 1896 include Danny Deever, Gunga Din, Mandalay, The Young British Soldier, and the Widow at Windsor pieces. Kipling writes in barrack slang, with choruses meant to be sung.

The poems praise endurance, mock officers and recruits, and record cholera camps, route marches, and the boredom between battles. Their rhythm and direct speech made them popular far beyond army readers. They remain the best-known poems of soldier life from the late Victorian empire, admired and argued over in equal measure.
28203-moods:
Louisa M. Alcott wrote Moods in 1864, before Little Women made her famous, as a novel of love and changing feeling. Sylvia, a young woman of strong moods, moves through a year of whims, a golden wedding, and a courtship that tests her heart. Alcott opens with Emerson's image of life as a string of beads, each mood a coloured lens.

Chapters follow Sylvia from afloat on a river to flood, field, and fire, then to wedding, honeymoon, and twilight years. Her choices, and the men who love her, ask whether feeling or duty should rule a life. The novel shows Alcott's early, serious side, beyond her children's books.
2831-a-bundle-of-ballads:
Henry Morley edited this anthology of old English and Scottish ballads for general readers, gathering songs that had passed from singer to singer before they reached print. Chevy Chase, the Nut-Brown Maid, Adam Bell, Barbara Allen, Sir Patrick Spens, and Robin Hood pieces sit side by side with laments, ghost songs, and comic tales. The contents list alone reads like a map of folk storytelling.

Each ballad tells its story fast, through dialogue and repeated refrains rather than description. Lovers part, outlaws escape, kings meet commoners in disguise, and the dead return to speak. Morley's selection gives a newcomer the core of the ballad tradition in one volume, with the old spellings and rhythms left close to the sources.
28340-birdseye-views-of-far-lands:
James T. Nichols wrote Birdseye Views of Far Lands, Des Moines, 1922, as a travel book for readers who cannot visit foreign lands. Nichols, author of Lands of Sacred Story, first printed much of the book in Successful Farming, a magazine with over 850,000 readers per issue, at their request. He began travelling with no thought of writing, and kept notes, sometimes copying sentences without credit.

Nichols admits no literary merit is claimed, and that credit cannot always be given where due. His aim is to be suggestive and helpful, showing places and peoples as they really are. The book offers a plain, earnest tour of the world for farm readers.
28424-tales-from-scottish-ballads:
Elizabeth W. Grierson's Tales from Scottish Ballads retells old Scottish ballads as stories for children, with four colour illustrations by Allan Stewart. First published in 1906 as Children's Tales from Scottish Ballads, the book was reissued in 1916 and included in Black's Boys' and Girls' Library in 1925.

Tales include The Lochmaben Harper, Kinmont Willie, The Gude Wallace, Muckle-Mou'ed Meg, Dick o' the Cow, The Heir of Linne, Thomas the Rhymer, Sir Patrick Spens, and The Gay Gos-Hawk. Grierson keeps the border raids, tricks, and romance of the ballads while turning verse into prose. The result is a lively doorway into Scotland's ballad tradition.
28467-samantha-at-coney-island-and-a-tho:
Marietta Holley, writing as Josiah Allen's Wife, published Samantha at Coney Island in 1911, with Samantha herself as narrator. The Coney Island microbe enters the quiet Jonesville home when Serenus Gowdey describes the resort's wonders, and Josiah begins to hanker for Coney.

First the family sails for Thousand Island Park and Alexandria Bay, where Josiah fishes, Mr. Pomper declares his intentions, and Faith meets romance. Then Josiah slips away to Coney Island, and Samantha pursues him through Steeplechase Park and Dreamland, surviving a fire before she finds him. Holley writes broad, dialect humour about marriage, travel, and temptation.
28625-battling-the-clouds:
Captain Frank Cobb's Battling the Clouds, or For a Comrade's Honor, published by the Saalfield Publishing Company in 1921, opens the Aeroplane Boys series. Fort Sill's aviation field quivers in mid-July heat, hangars gleam white, and planes hop along the ground like huge dragonflies. Splendid young airmen leap out, pushing off goggles and leather headgear after practice.

Two boys in a hangar's shade ignore the show, intent on a screen-wire cage holding an immense, furious tarantula. The spider hurls itself at a stick, and the boys debate what to do with a pet no mother or commanding officer will house. Later volumes promise an aviator's luck, the Camp Knox plot, and a flight in a dirigible.
28735-the-radio-boys-with-the-revenue-gu:
Gerald Breckenridge's The Radio Boys with the Revenue Guards, published by A. L. Burt of New York in 1922, follows three Long Island boys. Frank Merrick, Jack Hampton, and Bob Temple, sons of wealthy parents on country estates, attended Harrington Hall Military Academy. Jack, a year older, graduated and spent a freshman year at Yale, while Frank, an orphan, lives with the Temples.

Last summer brought a father's capture by Mexican rebels in New Mexico and a smuggling gang in San Francisco. This summer opens quieter, at a powerful radio station Mr. Hampton built under a government license for an 1,800-meter wavelength. Frank lounges in the doorway, Jack listens in, and the Atlantic sparkles a mile away. Readers get wireless adventure, with revenue guards ahead.
29157-the-coinages-of-the-channel-island:
Lieutenant-Colonel B. Lowsley of the Royal Engineers published this numismatic study in London in 1897. Lowsley, already known for work on the coins of Ceylon and on seventeenth-century Berkshire tokens, turns to Jersey and Guernsey and their neighbors. The Channel Islands, close to France but British, developed coinages of their own.

Chapters cover general observations, the earliest island coins, Roman coins found there, and early imported coins and their values. Later sections treat the coats of arms, Jersey silver tokens of 1813, copper and bronze coinages from 1841, and Guernsey coins from the Middle Ages. Readers get a specialist catalogue and history, precise and illustrated by its tables, for collectors and island historians.
29297-among-the-brigands:
James de Mille, professor and popular author, published this adventure in 1871 with Lee and Shepard in Boston. De Mille sets his tale among Italian brigands, opening with a stranger in a strange land, a citadel of trunks, and a siege. A tremendous uproar follows, with kicks, thumps, smashed chairs and tables, a cry for help, and the voice of David.

Later chapters follow David and Clive through a joyous ride, a meditation on a classic past rudely interrupted, and a drive into the country toward Sorrento and eternal summer. The cave of Polyphemus enters the itinerary. Readers get a boys' adventure of Italy, lively and episodic, where classical scenery meets very unclassical danger.
29427-lotus-buds:
Amy Wilson-Carmichael was a Keswick missionary of the Church of England Zenana Missionary Society. She published this book in London in 1912 with Morgan and Scott. It was copyrighted in 1909. It carries fifty half-tone illustrations from photographs specially taken for the work. Carmichael worked at Dohnavur in the Tinnevelly district of South India, and the book tells of the children in her care there.

Chapters run from Lotus Buds and Opposites through The Scamp, The Photographs, and Tara and Evu, to Principalities, Powers, Rulers, and How the Children Come. Later chapters ask Failures, tell how God heard and answered, and offer a story of comfort. Readers get a missionary memoir, tender and devout, about children sheltered at Dohnavur and the work of raising them.
29535-the-hands:
Richard Sternbach's vignette, printed in Amazing Stories, tells the story of creation and destruction in a few hundred words. A gigantic figure sits atop a mountain, his beard a white flag in the wind, able to dam the river below with a finger. Across the plains fires glow, the mountain trembles from explosions a thousand miles away, and a muffled cry rolls down the hillside. A smaller figure appears beside him, sad and pleading.

Try again, father, the smaller one says. Give them another chance. Just once more. The old one shakes his head: it would be the same, they would do it again. Sternbach asks, in miniature, whether creation can bear its own failure. Readers get a brief, majestic fable about mercy, judgment, and a father's grief.
29674-higher-education-and-business-stan:
Willard Eugene Hotchkiss gave these lectures on the morals of trade at the University of California, and they were printed in 1918. At the time he led business teaching at the University of Minnesota. The lectures belong to the Barbara Weinstock series, which asked scholars and men of affairs to weigh the moral law in trade.

Hotchkiss asks what schools owe the world of trade, and what trade owes in return. New wealth and new firms were remaking American life then. He opens in a California garden, with his small child at play, then turns to the classroom, the office, and the public trust. His case is that sound trade needs trained minds, plain dealing, and a sense of duty to buyers, workers, and the town.
29730-desserts-and-salads:
Gesine Lemcke, principal and owner of the Brooklyn and New York Cooking Colleges, wrote this cook book on desserts and salads. It carries copyright dates of 1892, 1896, and 1918, and this edition is dated 1920. Lemcke also wrote The European and American Cuisine and a book on chafing-dish recipes. Her motto stands on the title page: eating is a necessity, but cooking is an art.

The book gives tested recipes for the sweet and cold ends of the meal, in the clear style of a teacher who ran cooking schools. Fractions, halves, and quarters mark its measures, and a transcriber's index was added to the text. It suits cooks who want the desserts and salads of a trained teacher, set out for home use rather than for show.
29991-the-boy-scouts-on-belgian-battlefi:
Lieut. Howard Payson wrote The Boy Scouts on Belgian Battlefields, printed in New York in 1915 by Hurst and Company, with pictures by Charles L. Wrenn. Payson was known for the Motor Cycle Series and a long run of Boy Scout books, from the Eagle Patrol to the Panama Canal and Mexico. This volume sends his scouts into the Great War's Belgian front.

Antwerp on the Scheldt, an aerial map-maker, and leaving for the front open the tale. Under the bridge, the desertion of Anthony, and the coming of the Uhlans follow, with fire and smoke and the duty of a scout. Mysterious signals, a field hospital, and the battle for the trenches lead to the badge of courage and mercy. An armored car, scout tactics, and the frog hunters close a brisk boys' war tale.
30095-at-the-crossroads:
Brace Northrup sits smoking and brooding in Doctor Manly's office after a serious illness, at the start of Harriet T. Comstock's novel about life choices. Manly, his friend as well as his doctor, watches a man who does not yet see that he stands at a turning point. Comstock's theme is plain from the first page: great turns in life are often rounded without notice, and only past the curve do we grasp what has happened.

Doubleday, Page published the Garden City volume in 1922, and Comstock, author of Janet of the Dunes and Joyce of the North Woods, keeps the focus on character, home, and moral weather. Invisible tides hurry her people on, and small choices gather weight until they change a life. The novel suits readers who like thoughtful domestic fiction about second chances and quiet courage.
30125-the-flute-of-the-gods:
Marah Ellis Ryan wrote The Flute of the Gods, printed in New York in 1909 by Frederick A. Stokes Company.

Twenty-four chapters carry the tale: the woman from the south, the day of the sign, and the journey of Tahn-Te. White seekers of treasure, Tahn-Te among strangers, and Tahn-Te the ruler follow, with the silken scarf and the story by the desert well. Yahn the Apache, shrines of the sacred places, and the maid of dreams lead to the coming of the Castilians and a pagan priest in council. The courier and the maid, the giving of the sun symbol, and the true vision lead through things revealed on the heights and the battle on the mesa. The Apache death trap, the choice of Yahn Tsyn-Deh, and the bluebird's call follow.
3013-the-birds:
Aristophanes wrote The Birds as a comic extravaganza, unlike his other surviving comedies in subject and conception. The introduction calls it a graceful, whimsical theme chosen for the opportunities it affords, and the footnotes explain Greek names, terms, ceremonies, and puns that would otherwise be lost. Two Athenians, Pisthetaerus and Euelpides, leave the city to found a city in the sky. The birds become gods, promising farmers that locusts will not eat their vine blossoms.

Owls and kestrels will devour the pests, and gnats and gall bugs will be kept in check. Pisthetaerus bargains with gods and men alike. The comedy still delights with its fantasy, wordplay, and the sheer daring of building Cloudcuckooland between earth and heaven.
30225-many-gods:
Cale Young Rice gathers travel poems under the title Many Gods, published by Doubleday, Page in February 1910 and dedicated to Finis King Farr, an old and dear comrade. All's well opens, with a proselyte recanting, love in Japan, maple leaves on Miyajima, a typhoon, Penang, and the pagoda slave following. Ships of the sea, Kinchinjunga, the barren woman, and a poem by the Taj Mahal carry the reader across Asia.

Later pieces visit a tropical garden, a shrine of shrines, a felucca, the Egyptian wakes, and the imam's parable, with songs of a sea farer and a song of the sects. A Shinto temple garden, far Fujiyama, Miyajima mountain, the Yang-tse-Kiang, a Parsee woman, Shah Jehan to Mumtaz Mahal, and a Cinghalese love lament widen the map. Rice, author of Nirvana Days, writes as a wandering poet among many faiths.
30340-the-passionate-friends:
H. G. Wells tells of passionate friends in a novel published by A. L. Burt in New York in October 1913, by arrangement with Harper and Brothers, under a 1913 copyright. Mr. Stratton writes to his son at middle age, his attitudes defined and his personal drama worked out, hoping that writing and reconsideration will clear and fix thoughts never fully stated. Boyhood follows, with intentions and the Lady Mary Christian, then her marriage and the war in South Africa.

Lady Mary Justin, beginning again, and chapters on the swarming business of mankind and the spirit of the new world carry the story forward. Mary writes, a last meeting follows, and an arraignment of jealousy closes the book, whose frontispiece recalls kisses of moonlight. Wells, author of Marriage, writes love, marriage, and modern life with earnest, searching intensity.
30347-adventures-in-the-philippine-islan:
Paul de la Gironiere recounts his long stay in the Philippine Islands from journals he kept after leaving France. The narrative was translated from French and revised by the author for this edition. He trains for medicine, earns a naval surgeon's diploma, and sails for Manila, where early voyages give way to a settled life at Jala-Jala.

Chapters follow cholera and massacre at Manila and Cavite, a rescue by Captain Drouant, narrow escapes, hunting trips, and tangled dealings with captains, traders, and local leaders. Gironiere writes as a witness to frontier routines, trade, risk, and social rank, mixing travel detail with personal anecdote rather than a formal history of the islands.
30351-the-cup-of-fury-a-novel-of-cities-:
Rupert Hughes sets this 1919 novel in cities and shipyards, following Marie Louise through a world where marriage, work, and public life pull in different directions. Her wry reflection that it would be nice to be married while staying single at the same time sets the tone for a heroine who wants both freedom and attachment.

Hughes moves between drawing rooms and industrial scenes, showing how wealth, reputation, and wartime industry shape private choices. The plot turns on love, pride, and the cost of trying to keep every option open. Illustrated in its first edition, the novel reads as a brisk social story about modern women, ambitious men, and the price of having it all.
3054-volcanic-islands:
Charles Darwin wrote Geological Observations on the Volcanic Islands from his Beagle voyage, covering St. Jago in the Cape Verde Islands, Fernando Noronha, Terceira, Tahiti, Ascension, St. Helena, and the Galapagos. Later chapters treat trachyte and basalt, the distribution of volcanic isles, Australia, New Zealand, and the Cape of Good Hope. An editorial note calls the observations original and admirably adapted to general readers in many parts.

Darwin describes siliceous sinter and jasper in detail, noting white, pearly, light varieties passing into pinkish quartz, and yellowish white kinds with earthy powder in small cavities. Both occur in masses in altered trachyte or in veins. The book remains a foundational work of volcanic geology, written before Darwin's evolutionary fame.
30819-old-roads-and-new-roads:
Published in London by Chapman and Hall in 1852, this little volume warns its reader at once that it will not travel in a straight line. Its preface, addressed to Gentle Reader, says that anyone hoping for direct railway travel will be disappointed, since the route is circuitous and the guide eccentric. The book claims the precision of neither Patterson nor Bradshaw, the oracles of swiftness and straight roads.

Instead it begs readers, while whirled along a new road, to loiter mentally on old roads and to weigh the ways of travel that contented their ancestors. Coaches were slow and pack-saddles hard, the preface says, yet travelers reached their inns in time and left pithy, profitable records. It is a charming, rambling book on roads, coaches, and the pleasures of going slowly in a fast age.
30837-a-city-schoolgirl-and-her-friends:
May Baldwin wrote this 1912 girls' school story for W. and R. Chambers in London and Edinburgh, with six colored pictures by T. J. Overnell. Baldwin had already written Corah's School Chums, Two Schoolgirls of Florence, and Sarah's School Friend, among others. Its twenty-nine chapters run from Hard Facts and the new laird of Lomore through friends in need, ups and downs, and a new life to lonely lodgings and kind-hearted Londoners.

Later chapters follow good manners, the Enterprise Club, Bleak House Hostel, young house-hunters, and a home again, with Eva, Vava, and Stella among the friends. One picture shows a girl running off, turning to wave her hand to her sister. Baldwin writes a warm, old-fashioned tale of city girls making their way, with friendship, character, and pluck at its heart.
30864-the-missing-tin-box-or-the-stolen-:
Arthur M. Winfield wrote this 1897 boys' adventure novel, published by M. A. Donohue in Chicago, about a missing tin box and stolen railroad bonds. The first chapter opens on a talk between Allen and Hardwick, who put the bonds at close to eighty thousand dollars, with the market rising. From there the plot turns on Hal, a brave youth who stands up for himself and determines to act when a serious charge falls on him.

Thirty-two chapters follow Hal through a blow in the dark, a plot against him, an accusation, and a narrow escape, with Laura Sumner, Felix Hardwick, and Allen in the mix. Hal defends a girl, plays a daring part, and at last faces Hardwick's dash for liberty and a surprising revelation. It is a fast, old-fashioned tale of pluck, honesty, and a boy clearing his name.
30931-the-ethnology-of-the-british-islan:
R. G. Latham, a doctor of medicine and fellow of the Royal Society, wrote this 1852 study of the peoples of the British Islands, published by John Van Voorst in London. Latham, a corresponding member of the Ethnological Society of New York, works from archaeology, history, and language to trace who lived in Britain and Ireland, and when. His book belongs to the early science of ethnology, before modern genetics and dating.

Chapter one treats present populations, Romans, the prehistoric period, the Irish elk, the stone period and its skulls and burials, and the bronze period with its gold ornaments, alloys, and dwellings. Chapter two weighs authorities for the earliest historical period, including Herodotus, Aristotle, Polybius, and Onomacritus. It is a dense, learned survey, best for readers of Victorian anthropology and British prehistory.
31083-the-recipe-for-diamonds:
C. J. Cutcliffe Hyne wrote this novel, published by Thomas Nelson and Sons in London, Edinburgh, and New York, in Nelson's Library. Its frontispiece picture shows Weems with his left arm stuck up, sighting a pistol over his elbow joint, a hint of the adventure inside. The volume stands uniform with other Nelson's Library titles of its day.

Companion volumes in the series include The Octopus by Frank Norris, White Fang by Jack London, The Princess Passes by C. N. and A. M. Williamson, The Man from America by Mrs. H. de la Pasture, and Sir John Constantine by Q. Others are A Lame Dog's Diary, Fortune of Christina M'Nab, The Battle of the Strong, and The Translation of a Savage. It is a popular adventure novel, presented in a handsome uniform series.
31211-cavalry-of-the-clouds:
Captain Alan Bott, writing as Contact, published Cavalry of the Clouds with Doubleday, Page in 1918, with an introduction by Major-General W. S. Brancker. Dedicated to the fallen of Umpty Squadron, Royal Flying Corps, from June to December 1916, the book is one of the first by a fighting airman about fighting in the air.

Chapters follow flying to France, the day's work, a summer joy-ride, spying out the land, a cloud reconnaissance, and the daily round. Letters from the Somme add a missing machine, a bomb raid, spying by snapshot, the Archibald anti-aircraft family, and battles and bullets. Brancker praises Bott's moderation, noting his squadron once held a record for heaviness of losses.
31292-a-year-in-the-fields:
A Year in the Fields gathers selections from John Burroughs's writings, illustrated from photographs by Clifton Johnson and published by Houghton, Mifflin, with a biographical sketch by Johnson. Burroughs was born April 3, 1837, in Roxbury among the western Catskills, in an unpainted one-story house amid heights, dales, woods, pastures, and fields. His later home Riverby on the Hudson anchors many of these pieces.

Contents run from a snow-storm and winter neighbors through a spring relish, April, birch browsings, a bunch of herbs with fragrant wild flowers and weeds, autumn tides, and a sharp lookout. Gentle, observant, and rooted in place, the selections show America's beloved nature essayist at his most companionable.
31409-timar-s-two-worlds:
Maurus Jokai's Timar's Two Worlds, published by M. J. Ivers and Company of New York in 1894 as part of the American Series, is a Hungarian romance in English translation. Book first, called "The St. Barbara," opens with the Iron Gate, a white cat, a dangerous leap with a mammoth, a strict search, and an ownerless island. Almira and Narcissa appear among its figures, and later chapters promise the voices of the night and the history of the islanders.

Timar, the hero, lives between two worlds: the busy world of commerce and the hidden world of the island. Jokai, Hungary's most popular novelist, fills the tale with adventure, romance, and moral contrast. Readers of nineteenth-century European fiction will find a sweeping, colorful story, where a man's double life becomes a test of honor and happiness.
31610-the-books-of-chilan-balam-the-prop:
Daniel G. Brinton's The Books of Chilan Balam, the prophetic and historic records of the Mayas of Yucatan, was presented as an address to the Numismatic and Antiquarian Society of Philadelphia in January 1882. It was printed in the Penn Monthly of March 1882, and published by Edward Stern and Company of Philadelphia. Brinton, vice-president of the society and member of the American Philosophical and Antiquarian Societies, treats a subject then quite new in American archaeology and linguistics.

Brinton argues that Maya civilization rose highest among the peoples of ancient America. He adds that among New World peoples, only the Mayas possessed a literature in letters and characters. It was preserved in volumes neatly bound, on paper made from tree bark and sized with durable white varnish. His pamphlet introduces the Chilan Balam books to English readers.
3206-moby-multiple-language-lists-of-com:
This file holds the Moby language lists, a set of public domain word lists of common words in many languages. The documentation notes trace them to the Ward word lists, among the largest free lists in the world when they joined the Gutenberg collection in 2007. They carry no accented characters or Unicode, as a newer file would. Instead they use phonetic spelling, so plain ASCII can hold them.

Such lists serve spell checkers, language learners, and software that must guess a text's tongue from its commonest words. Readers opening the file will find data, not essays: word after word, language after language, in a form built for lookup. The set remains a useful record of how free language data was shared before Unicode became the norm.
32090-the-curlytops-snowed-in-or-grand-f:
Howard R. Garis's children's story, published by Cupples and Leon Company with a 1918 copyright, sends the Curlytops into winter. Garis, author of the Curlytops series, the Bedtime Stories, and the Uncle Wiggily series, supplied this volume with drawings by Julia Greene. Its subtitle promises grand fun with skates and sleds, and its frontispiece shows Ted's sled running away down a dangerous slope.

The contents run from a letter from Grandpa and a runaway sled, through Nicknack on the ice and a snow house, to Nicknack seeing himself and a snow man. The Curlytops series already included the children at Cherry Farm, on Star Island, and at Uncle Frank's ranch. Readers get a cheerful winter adventure for young children, where snow, ice, and a runaway sled provide the excitement.
32323-northern-diamonds:
Frank Lillie Pollock's Northern Diamonds was published in Boston and New York by Houghton Mifflin in September 1917. It first appeared in Youth's Companion as a serial and sequel, reprinted here by permission of that periodical's proprietors. Its illustrations, from drawings by Harry C. Edwards, include a frontispiece of a can lowered cautiously by a string, and boys busy at work. They continue with a cabin claimed aloud, a boy dragged up protesting with snow rubbed on his ears, and a sack flung into a man's lap.

Its first chapter opens near eleven o'clock at night, when someone knocks at Fred Osborne's room door. Fred, expecting no caller at that hour, had paid no attention to the boarding-house doorbell ringing downstairs or to feet ascending the steps, and hastens to answer. Readers get a boys' northern adventure, winter, cabins, and a mysterious sack, where a late knock starts the story.
32424-arthur-o-leary-his-wanderings-and-:
Charles James Lever's Arthur O'Leary, edited by his friend Harry Lorrequer and illustrated by George Cruikshank in a new edition published in London in 1845, follows a wanderer through many lands. Chapters range from the Attwood and the Boar's Head at Rotterdam to Van Hoogendorp's tale, Antwerp, and the Fischer's Haus. Mr. O'Kelly's tale, table traits, a dilemma, and a fragment of forest life follow.

Later chapters cover chateau life, the abbé's story, the chase, a narrow escape, and a mountain adventure. A soldier of the empire, the retreat from Leipsic, Bonn student life, spas, grand dukedoms, and a gambling room carry O'Leary onward. Lever mixes travel, anecdote, and moralising in a rambling, genial novel of European life after Napoleon.
32466-the-wouldbegoods:
E. Nesbit's Wouldbegoods, copyrighted in 1900 and 1901 and dedicated to her son Fabian Bland, follows a band of children determined to be good, with mixed results. Contents include the jungle, the wouldbegoods themselves, Bill's tombstone, the tower of mystery, the water-works, and the circus. Later adventures make them beavers, or young explorers Arctic or otherwise, and bring a high-born babe, a fox hunt, and a sale of antiquities.

A benevolent bar, Canterbury pilgrims, dragon's teeth or army-seed, and Albert's uncle's grandmother, or the long-lost, carry the fun onward. Reginald B. Birch's illustrations, including a frontispiece of a patriotic speech, accompany the tales. Nesbit writes with humour about children's plans, grown-up rules, and the gap between good intentions and good outcomes.
32696-planet-of-the-gods:
Robert Moore Williams sends the Third Interstellar Expedition to Vega, where astronomer Ron Val finds at least two planets, one with air and water in lakes. Commander Jed Hargraves and his crew land in hope of intelligent life, a prize astronomers had long deemed rare.

On the surface they meet folk led by Thulon, who seem to know more than strangers should, and a damaged ship becomes the prize in a struggle for control. A device called the negatron, and knowledge passed from a dead crewman, may decide whether the visitors leave, fight, or stay.
32767-some-specimens-of-the-poetry-of-th:
The Reverend Evan Evans, known as Ieuan Prydydd Hir, translates specimens of the poetry of the ancient Welsh bards, with notes on historical passages and short accounts of men and places. The volume reprints Dodsley's edition of 1764, published by John Pryse at Llanidloes.

Evans argues that no European nation holds richer remains of ancient genuine verse than the Welsh, and he offers them without setting them in competition with Ossian. Welsh originals stand beside the translations, praising Llewelyn and singing in the manner of Aneurin. Letters with Thomas Percy weigh fairy, elf, and goblin superstitions, and ask whether English metrical romances drew on old British fables.
3280-cap-n-warren-s-wards:
Joseph C Lincoln, author of The Depot Master and The Woman Haters, writes this Cape Cod novel of guardianship. Cap'n Warren's wards give the book its title and its problem: a seaman turned guardian, with young charges to raise and a village watching every choice. Edmund Frederick supplied the illustrations for the 1911 Appleton edition.

An early illustration shows Captain Warren risen from his chair and facing a woman, mid-argument, on page forty-eight. That scene sets the book's tone: plain talk, stubborn kindness, and comedy from duty. Lincoln writes his coast with affection, and the wards' fortunes, like the captain's, are settled by character rather than by luck.
32832-piper-in-the-woods:
Philip K. Dick tells of a biological impossibility at Earth's garrison on Asteroid Y-3: men becoming plants. Doctor Henry Harris examines Corporal Westerburg, a healthy young man of twenty-six, two years out of Training, who insists he has been a plant for several days.

Westerburg will not say how he became a plant, or whom he promised not to tell. Harris learns the delusion is spreading, with almost thirty cases among three hundred men. The men see a forest from their buildings and visit it on rest days, returning changed. Harris concludes that only growing self-awareness will make the Pipers vanish.
32853-in-the-cards:
Alan Cogan tells of the Grundy Projector, a device for trips about two years into the future, in this story from Galaxy Science Fiction of June 1956, illustrated by Emsh. Everyone uses one: students check examinations, couples count future children, and businessmen size up prospects.

The narrator, engaged to Marge, travels to their future home in the dome housing area and watches his future self and Marge fighting and screaming, hating each other after only two years. Society reshapes itself around foreknowledge, with newspapers carrying future sections and courtship done by looking ahead. Rog Owens at last names the trap: the projectors fixed the future, because whatever people saw, they let happen.
32946-where-the-pavement-ends:
John Russell's Where the Pavement Ends, copyrighted in 1919 and later filmed as a Rex Ingram-Metro picture, is a novel of the South Seas and the edge of civilization. Its contents open with The Fourth Man, and the story moves beyond paved streets and settled order into a world of traders, islanders, and men testing themselves far from home. An epigraph from Comus sets a tone of dark leaves that bear a bright golden flower in another country.

Russell, author of In Dark Places, writes adventure with a keen eye for place and character, and the novel's film success shows how vividly its scenes played. The book belongs to the popular adventure fiction of its day, mixing romance, danger, and the lure of distant shores. It remains an engaging period novel for readers who enjoy a story that leaves the city behind.
33319-zigzag-journeys-in-europe-vacation:
Hezekiah Butterworth's Zigzag Journeys in Europe, subtitled Vacation Rambles in Historic Lands, takes young readers on a winding tour of the continent. Published in Boston in 1882, with copyright in 1879, it aims to give boys and girls a lively sense of historic places, from boy-kings to old battlefields and cathedrals. The journey zigzags by design, following interest rather than a straight route.

The book's charm lies in its blend of story, history, and travel talk, with pictures to guide the eye. Butterworth writes as a friendly guide, pausing at each site to tell its tale. For young travelers and armchair tourists, it is a pleasant, old-fashioned companion to Europe, full of facts worn lightly and wonders kept fresh.
33438-sea-hounds:
Lewis R. Freeman's Sea-Hounds, published in New York in 1919, tells of British battle-ships on patrol in the Great War. Freeman, a lieutenant in the Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve, writes with photographs by himself, and dedicates the book to Commodore Sir Douglas Brownrigg. His frontispiece shows battle-ships on patrol, a scene that sets the book's naval tone.

The book's power lies in its first-hand, photographic record of sea war, from patrols to battles, told by a man who served. Its tone is vivid and patriotic, suited to readers of naval history. For those who love the sea in wartime, Sea-Hounds offers a stirring, well-illustrated account of the fleet that kept the seas.
33579-last-words:
Stephen Crane's Last Words, published in London in 1902, gathers stories and sketches from across his short career. The contents move from the reluctant voyagers of the opening tale through Spitzbergen stories and Wyoming Valley tales of the Revolution, to London impressions.

Later sections add miscellaneous tales of desertion, chance, poker, and war, closing with reflections on the moon and the mountain voice. The collection shows Crane's range: ironic humor, sharp visual description, and sympathy for people caught in awkward or dangerous moments. It is a good single volume for readers meeting Crane beyond his famous war novel.
33593-orchids:
James O'Brien, secretary of the Orchid Committee of the Royal Horticultural Society, writes the orchid volume of the Present-Day Gardening series, edited by R. Hooper Pearson. The series offered practical, popular volumes on single plant groups, from sweet peas and pansies to daffodils, carnations, rhododendrons, lilies, apples, pears, and roses. O'Brien's book brings specialist knowledge to amateur growers.

Readers learn how orchids grow, how to house and care for them, and which kinds suit ordinary greenhouses and windows. The volume reflects a period when orchid growing was moving from wealthy collectors' glasshouses toward wider enthusiasm. Gardeners interested in orchid history and cultivation will find a clear, period guide, written by a recognized authority of the day.
33616-the-way-of-the-gods:
John Luther Long, author of Madame Butterfly, writes a novel of Japan in this 1906 book. Thirty-four chapters move from a bronze god who may speak but once in a thousand years through Nippon Denji, the flying of the August carp. An eta outcast, an emperor, Miyagi field, faded glory, and a reincarnation widen the story.

Long blends Japanese legend, Russo-Japanese War echoes, and romance, following soldiers, gods, and lovers toward pity and afterward. His dedication honors one who owns joy because he bought it with sorrow. Readers interested in early American writing about Japan will find a rich, if period-bound, imagination of its myths, honor codes, and spiritual world.
33679-seeds-of-michigan-weeds:
W. J. Beal, botanist at Michigan Agricultural College, prepared this 1910 experiment station bulletin on the seeds of Michigan weeds. Issued as Bulletin 260 of the Division of Botany, it was sent free to newspapers in the state and to interested farmers on request. That was part of the station's mission to put agricultural science into practical hands.

The bulletin helps readers identify weed seeds, a first step in keeping them out of crops and seed stocks. Its descriptions and illustrations serve farmers, seed dealers, and students of Michigan flora. As a document, it also shows the early land-grant university at work: research translated directly into bulletins for the people who needed it, in plain language and at no cost.
338-old-indian-legends:
Zitkala-Sa, a Yankton Sioux writer, retells Dakota legends for children and adults. Old Indian Legends opens with Iktomi the spider fairy, in brown deerskin leggings and beaded moccasins. His painted face and red-banded braids mark him as a trickster.

Iktomi meets ducks, muskrats, coyotes, and fawns, and always learns too late. The badger and the bear, the tree-bound red eagle, and Iya the camp-eater follow. Zitkala-Sa's English keeps the tales' humor and warning. The collection preserves Dakota storytelling in print. Zitkala-Sa later fought for Native rights in Washington.
33834-air-service-boys-over-the-rhine-or:
Charles Amory Beach sends his Air Service Boys over the Rhine in this 1919 Saalfield adventure, illustrated by Robert Gaston Herbert. Tom Raymond and Jack Parmly wear the uniform of the Lafayette Escadrille near hangars somewhere in France. They watch a small fleet of Caudrons return from a night raid over German ammunition dumps and troop centers. They count anxiously lest any of their boys be missing. Twenty-five chapters follow double news, anxious days, Paris, suspicions, and bombardment.

Later chapters bring the Rue Lafayette ruins, Tom's father, a missing Mr. Raymond, a dud, a monster cannon, perilous service, a spy, a picked squadron, a cloud battle, queer lights. Beach writes brisk wartime aviation adventure for boys, with blowing up a German munition factory as its emblematic thrill.
3710-an-unprotected-female-at-the-pyrami:
Anthony Trollope turns a Nile tour into comedy in this short tale of an Englishwoman who travels Egypt without a male escort. Miss Dawkins, brisk and sure of herself, joins a party bound for the Pyramids, and her fellow travelers spend as much time judging her freedom as they do gazing at tombs. The narrator watches the clash with amused detachment, noting how a woman alone draws comment at every halt.

Donkey boys, racing lads, picnic hampers, and the long climb up the stone sides fill the day with bustle. Miss Dawkins proves more taken with Mount Sinai, which is nowhere in sight, than with the Pyramids before her nose. The tale is a light study of manners abroad, where pride, gossip, and good humor mix under a hot sun.
3791-the-reign-of-law-a-tale-of-the-kent:
James Lane Allen sets this Kentucky novel in the hemp fields where Anglo Saxon farmers first won a foothold in the western wilderness. The story opens in 1782, with hemp growing tall beside the walls of Bryan's Station while backwoods riflemen Tomlinson and Bell ride to rouse the settlements and save the west. From that frontier summer Allen follows farm folk through seasons of labor, faith, and change.

A later scene shows a workman in the dead fields at a winter sunset, dust on his throat and eyes, gazing at a great light on the dark red horizon. The moment kindles a spiritual passion in him, a flame of immortal things alive in his soul. The novel suits readers who like regional fiction where land, work, and inner life grow together.
4042-mozart-the-man-and-the-artist-as-re:
A portrait of Mozart built from his own letters shows the composer as a working artist, arguing craft with his father. Writing from Vienna in November 1780, he debates the Ghost's speech in Hamlet, warning that a speech too long breaks belief on stage.

The voice, he insists, must be terrifying and real, and length itself can betray the fiction. Such letters reveal Mozart the dramatist, thinking about effect, timing, and truth in music and theater. Readers who love Mozart will enjoy meeting him in his own plain, sharp words, far from legend.
413-ballads:
Robert Louis Stevenson gathers narrative poems of far seas and old wars in this 1895 volume. The Song of Rahero tells a Tahitian legend of slaying and revenge, with notes on island custom. The Feast of Famine treats Marquesan rites, while Ticonderoga follows a Highland name across the Atlantic to war.

Shorter pieces include Heather Ale, a Galloway legend of a secret brew, and Christmas at Sea, a sailor's bleak holiday. Stevenson writes in strong, rolling verse, keen on place and fate. The book shows his gift for tale-telling in meter, from Pacific isles to Scots glens.
4205-berlin-and-sans-souci-or-frederick-:
L. Muhlbach's historical romance turns to Frederick the Great and the dancer Barbarina at Sans-Souci. Resting half reclined on a small crimson divan, arms crossed over her breast, Barbarina fixes blazing eyes on the intruders and sits petrified in stubborn silence.

She has the glance of a panther prepared for death or to slay her enemy, while the king stands quiet and waiting. Muhlbach builds court, love, and power around the Prussian king's circle. Readers who enjoy royal romance will find a dramatic tale of a dancer who would not bend.
4248-the-problem-of-the-ohio-mounds:
Cyrus Thomas wrote this study to answer a much-debated question. Who built the great earthworks of Ohio? Were they the work of a lost race, or of native peoples known to history? He weighs historical evidence, burial customs, and pottery. He also weighs stone tools and the layout of the mounds.

Later chapters test the case for the Cherokees as mound builders. They cover links to the Tallegwi of tradition. They compare mound burials with Indian practices, such as burial in dwellings and the use of fire. Thomas argues from close comparison rather than legend. The book remains a clear statement that the mounds belong to Indian history.
438-underwoods:
Robert Louis Stevenson gathers verse in English and Scots in this volume, first shaped in the 1880s. Book one holds songs of the road, the sea, and friends, including the famed Requiem with its wide and starry sky. Later books turn to Scots speech, doctors, and the sickroom, with a dedication praising physicians as a rule.

Stevenson stole his title from Ben Jonson and owned the theft with a jest. His lines mix cheer, grief, and a traveler's restlessness. The book shows a poet of wide range, at home in both tongues, and it keeps his most quoted short poems in one place.
4381-the-aran-islands:
John M. Synge wrote this account of the Aran Islands off the west coast of Ireland, thirty miles from Galway. He begins with simple geography: Aranmor, nine miles long; Inishmaan, round and three and a half miles across; and Inishere, slightly smaller. Kilronan, the chief village, has changed with the fishing industry.

Synge lived among islanders, listening to their stories, songs, and speech, and watching their work in boats, fields, and stone-walled plots. The book records a world of Irish language, belief, and hardship, before modern change swept it away. It is both travel writing and a source for Synge's plays, and it remains a classic of Irish literature.
454-the-breitmann-ballads:
Charles G. Leland writes comic ballads in the voice of Hans Breitmann, a German-American whose broken English and high spirits carry him through beer halls, battles, and love affairs. The dialect is the joke and the charm. Leland created Breitmann in the 1860s, and the ballads ran in magazines before book form.

Leland, a scholar of folklore as well as a humorist, lets Breitmann blunder through American life with cheerful confidence. The ballads were hugely popular in their day, and they still read as a lively piece of nineteenth-century humour. Breitmann's German-English, full of comic errors, made him a favourite of American readers.
5149-gold-of-the-gods:
Arthur B. Reeve's mystery follows Professor Craig Kennedy into a case of Peruvian treasure, beginning with a Peruvian dagger and a soldier of fortune. Chapters run through treasure hunters, a Wall Street promoter, the curse of Mansiche, arrow poison. A poisoned cigarette appears, as Kennedy uses X-ray readers, paper fibres, and shoe prints to trace the crime.

The novel mixes archaeology with modern detection, moving from museum relics to laboratory tests. Readers of Reeve's scientific detective stories will find the usual brisk plotting. Inventive gadgets drive a treasure hunt that turns deadly.
5420-rab-and-his-friends:
John Brown, a Scottish doctor and writer, gathered these sketches and stories around the figure of Rab, a faithful dog, and his master. The collection grew from a lecture Brown gave in his native village of Biggar, where he chose to tell his listeners the story of Ailie, a patient whose courage stayed with him. Warmth, humor, and simple human feeling run through the pieces.

The best-known tale follows a poor Scottish family and their dog through illness and loss, told in Brown's plain, affectionate voice. Other sketches recall doctors, villagers, and everyday kindness in nineteenth-century Scotland. Readers looking for gentle, humane storytelling will find this short book moving without ever turning sentimental.
5762-grammar-and-vocabulary-of-the-lau-l:
Walter Ivens presents a grammar and vocabulary of the Lau language of the Solomon Islands, published by the Carnegie Institution. The transcriber notes that some fine distinctions of neighboring Saa orthography were lost, while Lau spelling stands as given. Ivens sets out sounds, word forms, and sentence patterns, then supplies a vocabulary for learners and field workers.

The book serves linguists, missionaries, and historians of the Pacific, preserving a record of Lau as spoken in its time. Readers will find a scholarly reference rather than a storybook, with paradigms and word lists as its core. Its value lies in documentation: a language community's speech, captured in print for study and for descendants seeking their heritage.
6164-the-life-of-the-fields:
Richard Jefferies gathers The Life of the Fields from magazine pieces, thanking editors who allowed reprints. The Field-Play appeared in Time, Bits of Oak Bark and The Pageant of Summer in Longman's Magazine, and Meadow Thoughts and Mind under Water in The Graphic.

Clematis Lane, Nature near Brighton, Sea, Sky, and Down, and January in the Sussex Woods came from The Standard, with other essays from art, nature, and London papers. Contents promise the pageant of summer, field play, acorn gathering, and rural dynamite. Jefferies writes country life with close eyes and a poet's patience.
6329-catalogue-of-british-columbia-birds:
The Provincial Museum at Victoria publishes this catalogue of birds proven to occur in British Columbia, with a preface that admits its incompleteness frankly. The north and northeast interior remain a valuable field for work, and distribution notes for some species stay thin. Since John Fannin's 1898 list of 339 species and subspecies, the compiler adds twenty-four more, with thanks to constant observers like A. C. Brooks of Chilliwack and the Okanagan.

Entries run in systematic order, with places and seasons noted. A red backed sandpiper is common in spring and autumn migration along island and mainland coasts, taken at Chilliwack. A semipalmated sandpiper is not uncommon on the coast and common at Metlakatla. The catalogue is a working list for naturalists, plain in form and rich in local record, valuable precisely because it names its gaps and its helpers.
6408-letters-of-anton-chekhov-to-his-fam:
Constance Garnett chooses from eighteen hundred and ninety letters published by Chekhov's family those that best show his life, character, and opinions, with a memoir abridged from his brother Mihail's sketch. Letters to his wife after marriage were not yet published when she worked. The sketch opens in 1841, when a serf of a Russian nobleman bought freedom for himself and his family. The price was three thousand five hundred roubles, seven hundred a soul, with a daughter Alexandra thrown in for nothing.

That serf's grandson was Anton Chekhov, and the nobleman's son was Tchertkov, the Tolstoyan. Chekhov writes to family and friends with a doctor's eye and a storyteller's brevity, reading Bourget's Disciple in Russian and judging him gifted, intelligent, cultured, and steeped in natural science method. Garnett's volume is a life in letters, where a grandson of a serf becomes Russia's clearest witness.
6418-five-little-peppers-and-their-frien:
Margaret Sidney dedicates this book to her daughter Margaret, who embodies Polly Pepper in girlhood for her friends. A preface explains that so many interesting friends of the Five Little Peppers deserved their own stories, and this volume gives them. A five o'clock tea opens, with Phronsie sitting in the middle of the stairs, Clem Forsythe, and Miss Taylor's working bee.

Grandma Bascom, a disappointment, a garden party, and a ten dollar bill follow, with trouble for Joel, Rachel, and doings at the parsonage. Rachel laughs at a fine lady's dignity, doubles up her thin figure, and goes off in a gust of mirth. Sidney writes warm family comedy, where friends widen the Peppers' world and kindness, not wealth, settles each trouble.
6480-on-the-study-of-words:
Richard Chenevix Trench, archbishop, delivers On the Study of Words as lectures, in a twentieth edition revised by A. L. Mayhew. Coleridge's motto opens it: language is the armoury of the human mind, holding trophies of past conquests and weapons of future ones. Trench urges something beyond books: not in books only, nor connected oral discourse, but in words contemplated singly lie boundless stores of moral and historic truth, passion, and imagination.

Lectures cover poetry in words, morality in words, history in words, rise of new words, distinction of words, and the schoolmaster's use of words. A mid passage notes how idiot came to be called innocent, one who does no hurt, assuming hurt and harm are men's chief employment. Trench writes philology as moral history, where each word carries a lesson worth learning.
6489-a-book-of-golden-deeds:
Charlotte M. Yonge asks what a golden deed is, then answers with stories from Alcestis and Antigone to the Vendeans. The cup of water, how one man saved a host, the pass of Thermopylae, and the rock of the Capitol open the book. The two friends of Syracuse, the devotion of the Decii, and Regulus follow. The brethren of Judah, the chief of the Arverni, and the last fight in the Coliseum follow. Guzman el Bueno, faithful till death, the keys of Calais, and Sempach follow.

The constant prince, the carnival of Perth, the crown of St. Stephen, George the Triller, and Sir Thomas More's daughter sit beside heroes of plague, gunpowder perils, and soldiers in snow. A mid passage shows a penitent emperor, crown, purple robe, and buskins laid aside, prostrate before Ambrose, who pronounces forgiveness in his Master's name. Yonge writes heroism for young readers, deed by deed.
6524-stray-birds:
Tagore lines up more than three hundred tiny poems, each no more than a few lines, like birds that land, sing, and fly on. Summer birds at a window, autumn leaves with no song, desert sand begging for a tune, and tears that keep smiles in bloom all pass in quick succession. The book takes its shape from that brief, bright movement.

No poem stays long enough to grow heavy, yet many leave a clear image or a sharp turn of thought behind. Love, loss, the earth, and the small wonders of a day are the chief subjects, handled with a light hand. Stray Birds suits slow reading, a page or two at a time, with room to pause between each flash.
6742-the-school-for-husbands:
Molière's School for Husbands, first played in Paris in June 1661, was the first play to use School in its title as a promise of a lesson. The notice explains that Molière wished hearers to know he meant to teach married men, not just to amuse them, and to answer those who called theatre harmful or trivial. Sheridan and others later copied the title trick.

Two brothers, one strict and one easy, raise two wards in opposite ways, and the strict man's ward teaches him a lesson in love. The verse moves briskly, with wit as its weapon. The School for Husbands is a clever, enduring comedy on how not to rule a wife.
6851-ruth-fielding-at-snow-camp-or-lost-:
Alice Emerson sends Ruth Fielding to Snow Camp, lost in the backwoods, opening with a lively time and a surprising appearance. A newspaper clipping, the strange behavior of Fred Hatfield, and a trip off for the backwoods follow, with a train ride, a runaway in earnest, and first days at Snow Camp. Long Jerry Todd, bears, frost games, and peril with a taffy pull fill the winter.

A telephone chase, a battle in snow, a besieging storm king, a snow shroud, and a double captivity test Ruth's pluck. Emerson writes with bright, clean humor for girls. Ruth Fielding at Snow Camp is a cheerful, snowy adventure of friendship and courage.
6895-the-camp-fire-girls-go-motoring-or-:
Hildegard Frey sends the Winnebago Camp Fire Girls on an automobile trip in September, told by the group's own reporter at Nyoda's urging. The girls have just come home from Onoway House when a runaway girl, met in some distress, sets their journey in motion. Sahwah jokes that only a ride in a patrol wagon was missing, and the tale keeps that high spirited tone throughout.

Much of the fun springs from small things, including the craze for tan khaki outing suits that summer. From evening stars over a window to roads, mishaps, and new friends, Frey follows a band of girls learning to fend for themselves on the open road. Campfire loyalty is their guide.
7001-history-of-the-philippine-islands:
Antonio de Morga's history of the Philippine Islands, translated by Blair and Robertson, runs from Magellan's discovery in 1521 to the start of the seventeenth century. Morga, alcalde of criminal causes in the Royal Audiencia of New Spain and counsel for the Holy Office, wrote his Sucesos in Mexico in 1609. This volume one, issued separately from the fifty five volume Philippine Islands series, adds descriptions of Japan, China, and adjacent countries.

Appendices treat the expedition of Thomas Candish, and facsimiles accompany the text. Blair and Robertson edited and annotated the translation for the Arthur H Clark Company in 1907. The book remains a first hand Spanish account of the islands, their trade, wars, and peoples, at the dawn of colonial rule.
7381-the-eustace-diamonds:
Anthony Trollope's novel turns on a necklace and a widow who will not give it up. Lizzie Greystock, married briefly to Sir Florian Eustace, claims the Eustace diamonds as her own property. The family lawyers insist they are an heirloom that must pass to the heir. Lizzie, charming and unscrupulous, fights her case in drawing rooms, in the press, and finally in court.

Around the diamonds gather suitors, a scheming clergyman, a loyal friend in Lucy Morris, and a London world eager for scandal. Trollope uses the dispute to satirize society's greed and its love of a good story, while keeping sympathy for the people caught in the machine. The novel is one of his Palliser-era masterpieces of social comedy, sharp, funny, and unsparing.
7473-lost-on-the-moon-or-in-quest-of-the:
Roy Rockwood, the house name behind many boys' adventure series, sends his heroes to the moon in this novel. The chapters tell the plan in order. First comes a wonderful story, then something about the heroes. Then come preparing for a voyage, an accident, and the work of an enemy. At last they are ready for the moon, and off at last. A field of diamonds near the Sea of Tranquility is the prize they seek.

On the moon come torches of life, the edge of a crater, a breakdown, and the dread of being lost on the moon itself. Mark is captured, Jack is puzzled, and Washington sees a ghost, in the breathless sequence boys' fiction loved. The book is a period piece of early space adventure, written when the moon still seemed a place a clever boy might actually reach.
7552-quotes-and-images-from-motley-s-his:
John Lothrop Motley's History of the Netherlands is the classic American account of the Dutch revolt against Spain, and this volume gathers its quotations and images. Illustrations show the siege of Antwerp, William of Orange, called the Silent, the Earl of Leicester, Alexander Farnese, Prince of Parma, and John of Barneveld. The Hague in 1566, the last year of peace, opens the story.

The quotations catch Motley's republican spirit: a pleasantry called voluntary contributions or benevolences, a good lawyer is a bad Christian, and a common hatred united the provinces for a time at least. In that republic, the notes add, it was a penal offence to talk of peace or truce. The collection is a doorway into Motley's great narrative of a small country disinherited by nature, winning its freedom.
7776-the-call-of-the-cumberlands:
Charles Neville Buck's The Call of the Cumberlands opens near the backbone of the Cumberland ridge, where sun hesitates above a sugar-loaf cone over Misery Creek. Light still crowns the hillsides while gloom thickens below, where water tosses in small cascades between mossy boulders.

A native would know the rough creek bed as a country road, though no traveler passes now, save a partridge calling Bob White and a cardinal flashing among pines. Through mountain speech and feud country, the novel follows families bound to these hills, and a call home that proves hard to refuse.
7801-five-little-friends:
Sherred Willcox Adams's Five Little Friends, pictured by Maud and Miska Petersham, follows Bob, Betty, Paul, Peggy, and little Dot at school and on vacation. Bob wears a brown suit, Betty a checked dress, Paul a white blouse, Peggy curls, and Dot bobbed hair, all under teacher Miss West.

One morning Miss West hides a large round parcel on her desk, and the children guess balloon or football, both wrong. Through classroom surprises, games, and holidays, the book offers small readers a warm, orderly world where five friends learn, play, and look out for one another.
7846-departmental-ditties-and-ballads-an:
Rudyard Kipling's Departmental Ditties and Ballads and Barrack-Room Ballads joins two early volumes of verse on empire, office, and army life. The first runs from army headquarters and a legend of the Foreign Office through Uriah, public waste, and a code of morals to the last department.

The second brings the Ballad of East and West, the King's Mercy and Jest, Boh Da Thone, Danny Deever, Tommy, Fuzzy-Wuzzy, Gunga Din, Mandalay, and the Widow at Windsor. The opening lines eat bread and salt beside the dead, a pledge of shared life that runs through both books.
8393-life-in-the-backwoods:
Susanna Moodie wrote Life in the Backwoods as a sequel to Roughing It in the Bush, her famous account of settling in Upper Canada. Where the earlier book told of arrival and hardship, this volume sketches from nature. Its epigraph says the later life of a settler family is painful experience in a distant land, made her own, whether grave or gay.

Moodie, author of Life in the Clearings and Flora Lyndsay, writes with a settler's eye for neighbors, seasons, and the slow work of making a home. Readers of Canadian pioneer literature get a direct, often sharp voice, unsparing about both the bush and the people who came to it. The book stands as a classic of immigration writing.
8441-between-friends:
Robert W Chambers published Between Friends in 1914. It opens with Drene, a man who has entered into the obscurity of himself, like a man reentering a darkened house and lying down, aware of sunlight, bird-calls, and breeze outside. Through twilit corridors of his mind, Chambers follows a bruised soul, in the psychological manner of his later novels.

Chambers, once famous for weird tales, turned in his later years to society and psychological fiction, and this novel shows that turn. Readers get a story of friendship and inner life, told in the lush, slightly overwrought style Chambers favored. It suits readers tracing how popular novelists handled the new psychology of the 1910s.
8534-daily-strength-for-daily-needs:
Mary Wilder Tileston selected Daily Strength for Daily Needs, following her Joy and Strength for the Pilgrim's Day and Quiet Hours. Each day gives verses for strength, opening on January 1 with they go from strength to strength, and first the blade, then the ear. That the full corn in the ear, under the motto, as thy days, so shall thy strength be.

Tileston's devotional belongs to the Victorian habit of a verse for each morning, chosen to carry readers through the day. The selections draw on Scripture and hymns, arranged by calendar. Readers who keep a daily devotional will find a classic of the genre, plain, brief, and meant to be read slowly, one day at a time.
8777-authors-and-friends:
Annie Fields recalls the writers she knew in Authors and Friends. Opening with Chaucer's company of the leaf, whose laurel chaplets keep beauty fresh and green against every storm. Her contents read like a literary guest list: Longfellow from 1807 to 1882, glimpses of Emerson. Oliver Wendell Holmes with personal recollections and unpublished letters, days with Mrs Stowe, Celia Thaxter, Whittier's life and friendships, and Tennyson with Lady Tennyson.

Fields writes as a hostess and friend, not a critic, preserving talk, letters, and small kindnesses from Boston's golden age of letters. Longfellow's chapter begins with lilac buds bursting their sheaths each year, a fitting image for memory's return. Readers of American literature will find warm, firsthand portraits, best read as companions to the authors' own works rather than as formal biography.
9088-thoroughbreds:
W. A. Fraser wrote this novel of horse racing in upstate New York, dedicated to his wife, a thoroughbred herself. The scene is Brookfield, a village pinched into quiet isolation by a century of growth around it. Into its calm bursts horse racing, unearthed by Reverend Dolman and led by John Porter, called Honest John.

Porter's father raced in old Kentucky for sport, and the son kept the love. Fraser follows bets, breeds, and village talk with warmth. The novel charms as a tale of sport, character, and a small town stirred by speed and pride.
922-sunday-under-three-heads:
Charles Dickens wrote this short work on Sunday, dedicated to the Bishop of London. He takes Sunday under three heads, asking how the day should be kept, and for whom. His target is the strict Sabbatarian view that would shut the poor out of innocent recreation, while the rich enjoy their own Sundays in private.

Dickens argues with humour and humanity for a Sunday that allows rest, fresh air, and simple pleasures to working folk. The pamphlet shows his early social conscience and his gift for pleading a cause in plain prose. It remains a lively piece of Victorian debate, on a question that still divides opinion.
931-the-bab-ballads:
W. S. Gilbert wrote these comic ballads under the pen name Bab, for the magazine Fun and later collections. Sailors, policemen, ghosts, and lovers tumble through topsy-turvy plots, told in brisk rhyme with a logic that turns sense on its head. The 1920 Macmillan edition gathers the set for a new generation.

Gilbert's humour is dry, precise, and absurd, and the ballads were the seed of his Savoy operas with Sullivan. Many types and jokes from the stage first appear here, in verse. The book is a treat for lovers of nonsense with a sharp edge, where rhyme and reason play a merry game.
933-more-bab-ballads:
W. S. Gilbert gathered more of his Bab Ballads in this companion volume, with tales such as The Bumboat Woman's Story, The Two Ogres, Little Oliver, Mister William, and Pasha Bailey Ben. Lieutenant-Colonel Flare and other comic heroes follow, each caught in a plot where logic leads straight to folly.

Gilbert's verse is brisk and witty, with rhymes that snap and morals that wink. The ballads show the same topsy-turvy world as the first set, where rank, love, and law are turned upside down. The volume is a further feast for Gilbert fans, and a fine sample of Victorian comic verse at its most ingenious.
9405-the-book-of-old-english-ballads:
George Wharton Edwards gathered this book of old English ballads, with decorative drawings and an introduction by Hamilton Mabie, in 1896. Contents include Chevy Chace, King Cophetua and the Beggar-Maid, King Leir and his three daughters, and Fair Rosamond. Robin Hood tales, Barbara Allen, Sir Patrick Spens, and The Nut-brown Maid follow.

Mabie's introduction opens with Chevy Chace itself, a woeful hunting in the border hills. The ballads sing of love, war, and fate in old, plain speech. The book remains a handsome gateway to the ballad tradition, for readers and singers alike.
9482-what-sami-sings-with-the-birds:
Johanna Spyri, best known for Heidi, wrote What Sami Sings with the Birds, here in Helen B. Dole's 1917 translation. Sami is a poor Swiss boy whose hard life leaves him few joys, save the songs of birds by Lake Geneva. The tale follows him from Old Mary Ann's care to his grandmother's house, through want and loss. Birds, heard each spring, mark his hope.

As Sami grows, he learns to sing with the birds, and song steadies him through hard times. Spyri keeps the prose simple and the feeling warm, with Swiss fields, brooks, and ash trees close at hand. A reader gets a gentle story of a child who finds courage in nature and music, and a fine short companion to Spyri's better-known Alpine tales.
9500-farm-ballads:
Will Carleton wrote Farm Ballads, a book of poems drawn from farm life and country folk. Carleton says he wrote them in the open air, on trains, and in editors' rooms, then printed them in papers where readers met them with favor. Friends across the country asked him to gather them in lasting form. The book answers that call with plain, heartfelt verse.

Poems sing of teams afield, harvests, home, and the toil and humor of rural days. Carleton's voice is simple and direct, with a farmer's eye for work and weather. A reader gets a beloved set of American country poems, warm and easy to read aloud, from a poet who knew the fields first hand.
9649-with-trapper-jim-in-the-north-woods:
Lawrence J. Leslie wrote With Trapper Jim in the North Woods in 1913, a boys' camp tale of the Campfire and Trail series. Three chums reach Trapper Jim's hunting lodge in the far North Woods, led by luck and pluck. Toby Jucklin, the stuttering lad of broad shoulders, steals early scenes. Chapters promise woodcraft, trapping secrets, and a silver fox.

Later chapters track a thief, a clog trail, and a bruin surprise, with smoking out intruders and steady shooting beside. The boys learn the woods by doing, not by books. A reader gets a rousing outdoor adventure, full of camp lore, animal craft, and the fun of chums on the trail.
9778-vane-of-the-timberlands:
Harold Bindloss wrote Vane of the Timberlands, a novel of Canada's woods, coasts, and lumber camps. Vane, a young man of the timber country, faces a friend in need, a breeze down a fir-scented inlet, and an afternoon ashore. Chapters follow Vancouver, a sail north, a first mishap, and the bush, with floods, trails, and an intercepted letter. Lucy Vane, Jessy, and Evelyn cross his path.

Later chapters bring a search, a flood, and convincing testimony, till Vane is reinstated at the last. Bindloss writes with brisk, outdoor verve. A reader gets a rousing Canadian adventure, full of canoes, camps, and a hero's fight for his name.
9852-the-man-from-the-clouds:
J. Storer Clouston's 1919 novel opens with a man found on a shore after coming down from the clouds. A small community takes him in, but a suspicious stranger, a doctor, and questions about who he is soon unsettle the place.

As the story moves into its second part, an idea, a little dinner, and a test bring the stranger's secret closer to exposure, with a pursuer named Bolton on the track. Clouston keeps the mystery light and brisk. Readers get a puzzle about identity, told with humor and a seaside setting.
9854-frank-roscoe-s-secret-or-the-darewe:
Allen Chapman's 1908 boys' book follows Frank Roscoe and his Darewell chums on a woodland holiday that turns into a mystery. The boys plan a dinner, stumble on a conspiracy, and watch as Ned is captured and hears strange talk in the woods.

Suspicions grow around a stranger in town and a neighbor's queer behavior, while the chums camp, race, and use a telephone wire to untangle the plot. Chapman writes in the brisk school-story manner of his day. Young readers get friendship, camping fun, and a secret worth guarding.
a-book-for-kids: Clarence James Dennis writes this book of verse for children in a playful Australian voice. Its poems visit a baker, a postman, a swagman, a pieman, and other figures of a local street. A kindly gentleman urges a boy to treasure his books and to keep them as companions rather than toys. The verses mix humor, rhyme, and everyday scenes that young readers can enjoy aloud.
a-book-of-golden-deeds:
A Book of Golden Deeds, published in 1864 by Charlotte M Yonge, gathers true tales of brave and selfless acts. Yonge was a popular Victorian novelist and writer for young readers. Rather than inventing a story, she collected real deeds of heroism from history and retold them in short, clear accounts meant to be remembered.

Each tale shows someone choosing courage, loyalty, or sacrifice at a hard moment, often at risk to their own life. Together the stories form a kind of moral gallery, offered to readers as examples worth copying. The book was a Victorian favorite for family and school reading, and it shows how the age taught character through story.
a-bundle-of-ballads:
Henry Morley edited this gathering of old English ballads, with an introduction on the minstrels who once carried such songs from house to house. The contents open with Chevy Chase in two versions, then The Nut-Brown Maid and the outlaw tale of Adam Bell, Clym of the Clough, and William of Cloudeslie. A glossary closes the book.

Robin Hood rides here, with Sir Patrick Spens, Edward Edward, Barbara Allen's Cruelty, The Children in the Wood, and Casabianca. Morley, a tireless editor of cheap classics for working readers, chose ballads for story and singability alike. The volume is a pocket library of the people's poetry, from border raids to ghostly lovers.
a-collection-of-ballads:
Andrew Lang edited this gathering of old English and Scottish ballads, first published in 1897 and reprinted in 1910, with an introduction and notes. The contents open with Sir Patrick Spens, the Battle of Otterbourne, Tam Lin, and Thomas the Rhymer. Many of the songs are centuries old and were carried by singing rather than by print.

The ballads tell of sea wrecks, border raids, fairies, ghosts, true love, murder, and betrayal, in short stanzas made to be sung. Names like Kinmont Willie, Johnnie Armstrong, and the Twa Sisters fill the list. Lang chose well-loved versions, so the book works as a first shelf of the folk ballad tradition.
a-countess-from-canada-a-story-of-life-i: Bessie Marchant tells a backwoods story of a countess from Canada. Its chapters move beyond the second portage through accidents, floods, business bothers, and a stranger who proves a friend. A woman of business, a first fishing, and new friendships fill the Canadian tale. Marchant writes an adventure of courage and resource in the northern woods.
a-string-of-amber-beads: Martha Everts Holden strings short essays like amber beads in this volume, copyrighted in 1893 and dedicated to Andrew Shuman, her literary adviser and truest friend. The contents run from I Didn't Think and Stay Where You Are through a cowardly mate, being shut in, and the circling year as a clock. Later beads include sermons from flies, the man who knows it all, bald heads and unequal chances, and human straws. Each bead is a small observation polished by wit.
about-orchids: Frederick Boyle chats about orchids in this 1893 volume with coloured illustrations, inscribed to his guide, comforter, and friend Joseph Godseff. The contents run from his gardening and an orchid sale through orchids themselves to cool, warm, and hot orchids, a lost orchid, an orchid farm, and orchids and hybridizing. Vanda Sanderiana fronts the book, with Odontoglossum, Oncidium, Dendrobium, Coelogene, Cattleya, and Cypripedium among the plates.
allan-and-the-ice-gods:
Allan and the Ice Gods, published in 1927 by H Rider Haggard, is the final volume of the Allan Quatermain saga. It forms the fourth part of a loosely linked series that began with Allan and the Holy Flower. Quatermain, Haggard's famous hunter hero, once more takes the hallucinogenic taduki drug, as he did in earlier novels of the series.

Under the drug, he finds himself reliving a past life as Wi, a civilized man living in the barbaric ice age as part of a clan of cavemen. The device lets Haggard set a modern mind inside a prehistoric struggle for survival. The book closes the Quatermain sequence with its strangest journey, into deep time rather than across Africa.
an-alphabet-of-old-friends: Walter Crane makes an alphabet of old friends for the nursery, with a zodiac to match, in pictures and short verses. Each letter brings a familiar figure or creature, drawn in Crane's bright, decorative style. The book is a charming example of Victorian picture-book art, meant to teach letters through delight.
an-unprotected-female-at-the-pyramids:
Anthony Trollope tells a tale of Egypt from the 1864 Chapman and Hall collection Tales of All Countries. He begins by remembering how Grand Cairo filled his young imagination from the Arabian Nights: fantastic houses, beautiful or cunning women, and good-natured, capricious monarchs. The grown traveler finds a different Egypt, full of tourists.

Among them is an English lady traveling without protector or chaperone, determined to see the Pyramids on her own terms. Guides, dragomans, fellow tourists, and a persistent admirer test her independence at every step. Trollope, who knew the tourist world well, mixes satire of travelers' pretensions with real sympathy for his heroine's nerve.
austin-and-his-friends:
Frederic H. Balfour published this book with Greening and Company of London in 1906. Its advertisement explains the experiment: old ghost stories were ghastly affairs of white sheets and clanking chains, enjoyed until bedtime. Balfour instead attempts a cheerful ghost story, fronted by a picture of Daphnis at the fountain.

Austin and his friends talk with, rather than flee from, the departed. One voice argues that the dead are not shadows of living men; rather the living move in a vain show until the spirit, the true substance, is set free. Darkness itself gains a revealing power in these conversations. Balfour, a writer on Taoism as well as fiction, turns the haunted-house tale into genial philosophy about death, light, and the soul's real life.
authors-and-friends:
